The Stack

Every major dependency this project takes on, and the one job each is there to do.

Every piece of this stack earns its place for a specific reason — nothing here is the default just because it's popular. A quick map of what's coming, grouped by the problem each one solves:

The server itself

  • Node.js — runs JavaScript outside the browser, as a standalone server process. Covered from first principles in the very next lesson.
  • Express — routing and middleware on top of Node's raw HTTP handling; the equivalent role Laravel's routing layer plays, minus everything Laravel bundles beyond routing itself.

Data

  • MySQL — the relational database, running in a Docker container so nobody needs to install it by hand.
  • Prisma — the ORM: schema, migrations, and a generated query client, covering the same ground as Eloquent but as a schema-first, standalone library rather than a framework feature.
  • Zod — validates the shape of incoming request data (a schema for request bodies, not for the database) before a controller ever sees it.

Auth

  • jsonwebtoken — issues and verifies JWTs: a signed, stateless token the client holds and resends, instead of Laravel's server-side session.
  • bcrypt — one-way password hashing, checked on login, never reversed.

Reacting to what happens

  • Node's built-in EventEmitter — no extra dependency; the backbone domain events (a ticket created, assigned, commented on, its status changed) get broadcast on.
  • nodemailer — sends the confirmation/notification emails those events trigger, to a local dev inbox (Mailpit, another Docker container) instead of anyone's real inbox while building.
  • socket.io — pushes those same events to a connected browser in real time, for a notification bell that updates without a page refresh.

Background work

  • BullMQ + ioredis (Redis) — a real job queue: retries, backoff, a separate worker process, scheduled/repeatable jobs. Used for the one piece of work nothing triggers directly — a periodic scan for tickets that have breached their SLA.

Hardening

  • helmet, cors, express-rate-limit — response headers, cross-origin rules, and request-rate limits: baseline defenses every production API needs, added once the core functionality exists to protect.

Testing

  • jest + supertest — the unit/integration test runner and its HTTP-request-against-app.js helper, introduced early and used throughout, not bolted on at the end.

Nothing above needs to make full sense yet — each one gets introduced properly, with working code, in the lesson where it's first needed. This is the map; the territory comes lesson by lesson.
